newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Raging inferno kills 39 on Hong Kong golden mile.
newsitem.headline: Raging inferno kills 39 on Hong Kong golden mile.

text.p: Fire engulfed a 16-floor shop and office block in a bustling Hong Kong tourist district, killing almost 40 people and injuring scores of others in the territory's worst building blaze on record.
The inferno flared up on Wednesday evening and raged through the night, gutting seven floors. Some 300 firemen and 50 fire engines battled the fire which took almost 24 hours to quell.
The confirmed death toll on Thursday reached 39, including one fireman, fire chief Peter Cheung said.

"We're still trying to identify bodies and relate those reported missing to those we already know have been killed but whose bodies have not yet been identified," colonial Governor Chris Patten told the Legislative Council.
Patten said 39 people were reported missing.
Officials said 80 people were injured. More than 110 were rescued. Of the injured, 59 were still in hospital.

The immediate cause was not known, but Cheung said he had received reports that welding work had been under way in the elevator area, on the ground floor where a Chinese arts and crafts store was located.
People trapped behind sealed windows on Wednesday night ripped off burning clothes, while others scrambled to safety.

A plume of flame lit up the sky above the famed Hong Kong harbour but later gave way to a black cloud of smoke that hung over the burned out Garley Building on Nathan Road, "golden mile" of the Kowloon peninsula tourist district.
Officials said 17 of the charred bodies were found on the 15th floor on Thursday morning.
"This was the most serious (building) fire and the one with the most number of deaths and injuries in the past 100 years," Cheung said.
Hong Kong's worst fire on record was in 1918 when 600 people were killed and 400 injured in a blaze at the Happy Valley Race course on Hong Kong Island.
A disaster in 1947 killed 149 people when a ship burned in the harbour. In 1953 a Christmas blaze killed an unknown number of people in a squatter village and left 60,000 homeless.
Officials sounded alarm bells about building safety, an issue of protracted debate in the densely populated territory.
"Since the old building does not have modern fire protection facilities, rescue operation is particularly difficult," Cheung said. Inquiries were launched into the blaze.
Patten visited the spot and later pressed for the speedy passage of legislation to tighten fire regulations. Many older buildings have few, if any, anti-fire devices.
In dramatic scenes, firefighters plucked survivors from the block, a maze of small offices, shops and workshops, and some were winched off the blazing roof by helicopter.
The fire broke out on Wednesday evening and rapidly engulfed the first four storeys of the building, before racing up the lift shaft to the top three floors, fire chief K.Y Tsang said.
The smoke blanked out the vision of daring helicopter pilots who flew dangerous missions, swirling over over the rooftops in clouds of dense acrid smoke, to winch away terrified survivors.
Others jumped from window ledges on to rescue ladders and some scrambled on to air conditioners, observed helplessly by friends and relatives far below in the crowded street.
One of the dead was a fireman killed while battling the blaze. Liu Chi-ho, 40, plunged down a lift shaft.

Another man fell from the building in a rush to escape. Witnesses said they saw him climb from a window and cling to an air conditioner. It gave way and sent the man tumbling several storeys to a canopy, where he lay crumpled and still.
